paragraphs.text: Across the Mediterranean, structures built by Roman engineers two thousand years ago are still standing. The dome of the Pantheon in Rome, completed around 128 AD, remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, and harbour walls built along the coasts of Italy have survived centuries of pounding waves. Modern concrete, by contrast, often begins to crack and crumble within fifty to a hundred years, particularly when it is exposed to seawater. For engineers, the contrast has long been both an embarrassment and a puzzle: how did builders without modern chemistry produce a material that outlasts our own?

Roman concrete, or opus caementicium, was not a single recipe but a family of mixtures. Its basic ingredients were lime, made by heating limestone, water, and volcanic ash, which builders packed together with chunks of rock or broken brick. The most prized ash came from the area around the Bay of Naples, near the town of Pozzuoli, and the Romans shipped it hundreds of kilometres for important projects. Writers of the period, including the architect Vitruvius, praised this ash for its ability to make mortar set hard even under water, although they had no way of understanding the chemistry behind it.

For much of the twentieth century, scientists assumed that the volcanic ash was the whole story. The ash contains silica and alumina, which react with lime to form a strong binding compound. This kind of reaction, known as a pozzolanic reaction after Pozzuoli, is also used in some modern cements. Yet this explanation could not fully account for the extraordinary durability of Roman marine structures. In fact, modern engineers deliberately avoid exposing concrete to seawater for long periods, because salt attacks the steel reinforcing bars inside and causes them to rust and expand, splitting the concrete apart.

A significant step forward came when a team led by the geologist Dr Helen Carver examined drill cores taken from ancient Roman piers along the Italian coast. Using powerful X-ray imaging, the team found that seawater seeping through the concrete had slowly dissolved parts of the volcanic ash. This allowed new minerals to grow in the spaces between the particles, including a rare, plate-shaped crystal called aluminous tobermorite. Rather than weakening the material, the seawater had made it stronger over time, as the interlocking crystals reinforced the structure. 'The Romans created a rock-like material that thrives in open chemical exchange with the sea,' Carver wrote. Tobermorite is extremely difficult to produce in a laboratory, where it typically requires temperatures of around 200 degrees Celsius.

A second mystery concerned small white lumps, a few millimetres across, scattered throughout many samples of Roman concrete. These lime clasts had traditionally been dismissed as evidence of careless mixing or poor-quality materials. However, a group of materials scientists headed by Professor Luca Ferrante has argued that the lumps were neither accidental nor a defect. Their analysis suggested that the Romans had mixed quicklime, a highly reactive form of lime, directly with the ash and water, rather than first combining lime with water to make a paste, as had generally been believed. This process, known as hot mixing, releases a great deal of heat, and it leaves behind lime clasts that are brittle and rich in calcium.

According to Ferrante, these clasts give the concrete a remarkable capacity to repair itself. When a tiny crack forms, it tends to travel through the clasts because they are weaker than the surrounding material. If water then enters the crack, it dissolves some of the calcium, which recrystallises as calcium carbonate and fills the gap. To test the idea, the team prepared samples of concrete made with and without hot mixing, deliberately cracked them, and then ran water through the cracks. Within two weeks, the cracks in the hot-mixed samples had completely sealed and water could no longer flow through, while the cracks in the other samples remained open.

These findings have attracted interest well beyond archaeology. The production of Portland cement, the key ingredient of modern concrete, is responsible for around eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, largely because limestone must be heated to about 1,450 degrees Celsius. Roman lime was produced at far lower temperatures, and a concrete that lasts for centuries would need to be replaced far less often, reducing emissions over a building's lifetime. Several start-up companies are now experimenting with mixtures that copy Roman techniques, and one has proposed a Roman-style recipe for sea walls designed to protect coastal towns from rising sea levels.

Nevertheless, researchers warn against seeing Roman concrete as a simple replacement for the modern material. Roman concrete is considerably weaker under compression than Portland cement, and it gains strength slowly, over months or even years rather than weeks. The Romans compensated for this by building massive, thick walls and avoiding the slender columns and long spans common in modern architecture. Moreover, because it contains no steel, Roman concrete performs poorly when it is pulled or bent. Most engineers therefore expect the ancient techniques to be combined with modern ones rather than to replace them: for example, by adding lime clasts to conventional mixtures to give them a degree of self-healing ability.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species and provide food, income and coastal protection for hundreds of millions of people. They are also in serious trouble. Since the 1950s, the world has lost around half of its living coral cover, and rising sea temperatures are now the greatest threat. When water becomes too warm, corals expel the tiny algae that live in their tissues and supply them with most of their energy; the corals turn white, a process known as bleaching, and if the heat persists they starve. In response, a global movement to actively rebuild damaged reefs has grown rapidly over the past two decades.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely used technique is known as coral gardening. Small fragments are cut from healthy colonies and grown in underwater nurseries, where they hang from ropes or from tree-like frames made of plastic piping. Raised off the seabed, the fragments are protected from sediment and from predators such as snails, and within a year or two they are large enough to be fixed back onto the reef with cement or cable ties. The method was pioneered in the Caribbean, where it was used mainly for fast-growing branching species such as staghorn coral, which can extend by more than ten centimetres a year. Volunteer divers with no scientific background can be trained to maintain nurseries, and this has made gardening popular with dive centres as well as conservation groups.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Gardening works less well for the massive, boulder-like corals that form the structural backbone of many reefs, since these may grow only a few millimetres annually. A solution emerged by chance. While working at a laboratory in Florida, Professor Kenji Watanabe accidentally broke a piece of brain coral into tiny fragments when moving it between tanks. Returning to the tank some weeks later, he found that the fragments had grown far faster than an intact colony would have done. The technique that followed, now called microfragmentation, involves cutting corals into pieces about one centimetre across and attaching them close to one another on a hard surface. As they grow, the separate pieces fuse together into a single colony, reaching in two or three years a size that would normally take decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Both gardening and microfragmentation, however, produce clones: every fragment is genetically identical to its parent. A reef made up of clones is vulnerable, because a disease or heatwave that kills one colony is likely to kill them all. For this reason, some scientists are turning to the corals' own reproduction. Many species release their eggs and sperm on a single night each year, in an event known as mass spawning. Researchers collect this material from the surface of the water, and the resulting larvae are raised in floating pools before being released onto damaged areas. The approach creates genetically diverse offspring, but the young corals face enormous losses: in the wild, fewer than one in a thousand settling larvae is thought to survive its first year. To address this, the Coral Futures Foundation has developed small ceramic 'seeding units' which are placed in the pools so that larvae settle on them; the units are then wedged into cracks in the reef, a method which the foundation reports has greatly increased the proportion of young corals surviving their first year.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more radical idea is to help corals adapt to warmer seas. Under an approach sometimes called assisted evolution, researchers identify colonies that survived recent heatwaves and breed them together in the hope of producing more heat-tolerant offspring. Others are experimenting with the symbiotic algae living inside coral tissue, cultivating strains that cope better with high temperatures. Early results are encouraging, but Dr Sofia Lindqvist urges caution. Selecting corals for a single trait, she argues, may come at a cost: colonies bred for heat tolerance could grow more slowly or become more susceptible to disease, and releasing them in large numbers could reduce the natural diversity of wild populations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever the method, restoration faces a basic problem of scale. Estimates of the cost vary from around US$10,000 to more than US$1 million per hectare, depending on the location and technique. Yet the Great Barrier Reef alone covers about 344,000 square kilometres, and the total area restored worldwide so far amounts to only a tiny fraction of that. Restored sites are also exposed to the same threats that damaged them in the first place: in several projects, carefully planted corals died during the next marine heatwave. Dr Amara Okafor, a marine ecologist, goes further, warning that well-publicised restoration projects may give governments and companies an excuse to delay cutting greenhouse gas emissions, which she describes as 'the only real solution'.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Few scientists, however, believe that restoration is pointless. Most now see it as a way of buying time: keeping key species and genetic diversity alive until, they hope, global temperatures are stabilised. On a local scale, restored reefs can also bring real benefits, attracting visitors to coastal communities and helping to reduce wave energy before it reaches the shore. To succeed, though, restoration must be combined with other measures, such as improving water quality and controlling overfishing, so that the corals which are replanted have a reasonable chance of survival.

passages.title: Machines and work: lessons from history

paragraphs.text: Every few decades, a wave of anxiety about machines and jobs sweeps through the industrialised world. In the early nineteenth century, English textile workers known as Luddites broke into factories and smashed the new mechanised looms. In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes warned of a 'new disease' he called technological unemployment. In the 1960s, the United States government set up a national commission to examine whether automation would leave millions without work. Today, the same fears have returned in response to artificial intelligence. What is striking is that each generation tends to regard its own worries as entirely without precedent. And because earlier fears did not come true, it is tempting to dismiss the current one as yet another false alarm. That, I will argue, is too comfortable a conclusion.

Consider the Luddites themselves. They are usually remembered as ignorant opponents of progress, and their name is still used as an insult for anyone who resists new technology. Yet most were skilled craftsmen, and their objection was not to machinery as such but to the way factory owners used it to cut wages and replace trained workers with cheap, unskilled labour. In the short run, their fears were well founded: the earnings of hand-loom weavers fell by more than half in the three decades after 1800, and many families were reduced to poverty. In the long run, of course, the textile industry employed far more people than before, as cheaper cloth created vast new markets. But the long run was of little comfort to a weaver who had lost his livelihood in 1812.

The optimistic case, which remains the view of most economists, rests on what is called the 'lump of labour fallacy': the mistaken belief that there is a fixed quantity of work to be shared out. Automation, the argument goes, lowers the cost of goods, which raises real incomes, and people spend that extra income on other products and services, creating demand for workers elsewhere. Entirely new occupations also appear. In 1900, around 40 per cent of the American workforce was employed in agriculture; today the figure is below two per cent, yet the country did not experience permanent mass unemployment. 'Every previous prediction of the end of work has failed,' observes the economist Professor Richard Haldane, 'and there is no reason to think this time will be different.'

Not all economists share this confidence. Dr Elena Marsh argues that earlier machines mainly replaced human muscle, so workers could move into jobs that required thinking, communication and judgement. Today's technologies, she points out, are increasingly able to perform exactly these cognitive tasks, which may leave displaced workers with nowhere to go. A related but more cautious position is taken by Professor Tomas Brandt, who argues that automation replaces particular tasks rather than whole jobs. In his view, whether employment rises or falls depends on a race between two forces: the elimination of old tasks and the creation of new ones. His research suggests that since the late 1980s, new tasks have been appearing more slowly than old ones have been automated, which may help to explain why wages for many workers in rich countries have barely grown.

Even when the optimists are right about the eventual outcome, the transition can be long and painful. Economic historians have noted that in Britain between roughly 1790 and 1840, output per worker rose steadily while average wages hardly changed, a period sometimes known as 'Engels' pause', after the writer Friedrich Engels, who documented the condition of the working class at the time. Moreover, the people who lose their jobs are rarely the ones who fill the new positions. A middle-aged weaver did not become a railway engineer; the new jobs went largely to his children or to younger workers from elsewhere.

In my view, the optimists and the pessimists share a common mistake: they treat technology as an external force whose consequences are determined in advance, as if the only question were how many jobs it will destroy. This has led to an obsession with forecasting. One widely cited study estimated that nearly half of all jobs in the United States were at high risk of automation; another, using different methods, put the figure at under ten per cent. Such enormous differences should make us sceptical of the whole exercise. The effects of a technology depend far more on the choices made by firms and governments: which technologies are developed, how they are introduced, and how the gains are shared. Particularly damaging, I believe, is what some economists call 'so-so automation': machines such as self-service checkouts, which replace workers while delivering only small improvements in productivity. These offer the worst of both worlds, since jobs disappear but little new wealth is created to generate demand elsewhere.

Policy, then, matters more than prediction. Governments can invest in education and retraining, fund research into technologies that complement human skills rather than replace them, and provide income support for those caught in the transition. None of this is guaranteed to work. But history does not tell us that everything will turn out well, nor that disaster awaits. What it does show is that the benefits of technological change are not automatically shared. The Luddites were defeated not because they misunderstood the machines, but because they had no political power to influence how those machines were used. That, rather than any forecast, is the lesson we should take from them.
